description: Five visitor-accessible rounds in the Algarve, Portugal: Nicklaus's Monte Rei in the east, the tournament-tested Quinta do Lago South and San Lorenzo, the cliff-top 16th at Vale do Lobo Royal, and the region's first championship course at Penina.
intro: The Algarve is Europe's most concentrated golf destination: a string of championship courses packed along Portugal's southern coast, all within about an hour of Faro Airport, and playable in every month of the year. The region's golf story starts with Sir Henry Cotton in the 1960s and runs through Nicklaus, Palmer-era tour events, and the Portuguese Open — and every course on this list welcomes visitors. Base in the central Algarve around Almancil and Vilamoura, allow at least four or five days, and book the big names well ahead: spring and October are the peak months, with mild temperatures and full tee sheets.

sections.heading: 1. Monte Rei Golf & Country Club, Vila Nova de Cacela
paragraphs: The eastern Algarve's anchor is the only Jack Nicklaus Signature course in Portugal. The North Course opened in 2007 on a 1,000-acre estate in the foothills of the Serra do Caldeirão, between the hills and the Atlantic near the Spanish border, and it closed for six months in 2026 for a renovation carried out with Nicklaus Design before reopening that September. It is a par 72 with five par threes and five par fives, and water comes into play on eleven of the eighteen holes — the defining feature of a layout that is consistently ranked the best in Portugal.

Monte Rei is a destination round rather than a filler: visitors are welcome on weekdays and weekends, but you must book in advance and bring a handicap certificate, with recommended maximums of 24 for men and 32 for women. Tee times run on twelve-minute gaps, so the pace is unhurried, and a shared buggy is included in the round. Treat it as the splurge of the trip — pair it with a night in nearby Tavira, one of the Algarve's prettiest old towns, and save it for the day you want your best golf, not your first round off the plane.

sections.heading: 2. Quinta do Lago South, Almancil
paragraphs: The South Course is the Algarve's great tournament course. Designed by William Mitchell in 1974, it winds through umbrella pines and lakes on the edge of the Ria Formosa Natural Park, and it hosted the Portuguese Open eight times between 1976 and 2001. Its signature championship memory is Colin Montgomerie's 1989 victory: he finished at 24 under par, eleven shots clear of the field, with a round of 63 along the way. The par-72 layout was extensively renovated in 2020 and was named Europe's and Portugal's Best Golf Course at the 2024 World Golf Awards.

Quinta do Lago is a resort, so the South Course is straightforward to book as a visitor — but bring an official handicap certificate, with maximums of 28 for men and 36 for women. It is the sternest test in the central Algarve, with long carries and water on the closing stretch, so play the tees that match your game and keep a ball in hand for the par-3 15th across the lake. It pairs naturally with the resort's North and Laranjal courses or with San Lorenzo next door, making Almancil the best base for a multi-round trip.

sections.heading: 3. San Lorenzo Golf Course, Quinta do Lago
paragraphs: Ask Algarve regulars to name the prettiest course in the region and many will say San Lorenzo. Designed by Joseph Lee with Rocky Roquemore and opened in 1988, it is laid out in a figure of eight through the protected Ria Formosa nature reserve, threading pine forest, saltwater lagoons, and marshland before finishing along the lagoon's edge. Golf World magazine once ranked it among the five best courses in Europe, and it was voted the best course in Portugal in a European Golf magazine poll. Pete Dye himself named it among his favourite courses on the Iberian Peninsula.

San Lorenzo is a resort course owned by the Dona Filipa Hotel, and hotel guests get the most favourable access — so if this is the round you most want, stay at the Dona Filipa in neighbouring Vale do Lobo. Everyone else books as a visitor through the club directly, in advance, with a handicap certificate and maximums of 28 for men and 36 for women. It suits the confident golfer who enjoys a thinking course: the corridors look generous until the wind gets up off the lagoon. Book it mid-trip, once you have your Algarve legs, and leave time after the round — the closing holes deserve to be savoured, not rushed.

sections.heading: 4. Vale do Lobo Royal, Almancil
paragraphs: Vale do Lobo was among the first resorts built in the Algarve, and its Royal Course carries the region's most photographed hole. Sir Henry Cotton designed the original golf here in the late 1960s; the current Royal layout dates from a 1997 rebuild by Rocky Roquemore, who combined several of Cotton's original nines into a single par-72 championship course. It hosted the Portuguese Open in 2002 and 2003. The headline is the clifftop par-3 16th, a shot of 218 metres over three red-sandstone cliffs to a green with the Atlantic behind it — one of the most famous holes in European golf.

Visitors are welcome on weekdays and weekends, with advance booking essential and a handicap certificate required (maximums of 28 for men and 36 for women). The Royal is shorter than the modern championship courses nearby and rewards controlled iron play and a sharp short game more than raw distance, so it suits a wider range of golfers than its reputation suggests. It sits about twenty minutes from Faro Airport in the heart of the central Algarve, so it works as either an arrival-day round or a late-trip showpiece — and the resort's Ocean Course makes an easy second round on the same trip.

sections.heading: 5. Penina Hotel & Golf Resort, Portimão
paragraphs: Every Algarve course owes something to Penina. The Sir Henry Cotton Championship Course opened in 1966, the first 18-hole course built in the region, laid out by the three-time Open champion on a flat old rice farm — the farm's drainage ditches became the course's unforgiving hazards. Cotton moved into the Penina Hotel and spent his later years refining the layout. The par-73 course hosted the Portuguese Open ten times, first in 1976, with winners including Nick Faldo, Miguel Ángel Jiménez, Sam Torrance, and Bernhard Gallacher, and it put the Algarve on the European golfing map.

Penina is a self-contained resort on a 360-acre estate near Portimão, in the western Algarve, and hotel guests can walk from breakfast to the first tee. The championship course is a stiff test with a maximum handicap of 28 for men and 36 for women, while the resort's nine-hole Resort Course gives mixed-handicap groups a gentler option on site. It is the history round of any Algarve trip: play it for the story as much as the golf, and pair it with the western Algarve's quieter charms — the fishing village of Alvor and the cliffs around Lagos are both a short drive away.
